newsitem.title: CHINA: History casts shadow over Sino-Russian partnership.
newsitem.headline: History casts shadow over Sino-Russian partnership.

text.p: Since the Russian bear bumped against the Chinese dragon on the steppes of northern Asia three centuries ago, relations between the giant neighbours have not been easy.

Even as China's state media on Thursday hailed this week's Sino-Russian declaration on a new world order, diplomats and analysts remembered the centuries of suspicion and animosity that have characterised ties.
"They have shared a very long border for thousands of years and it is not often that they have agreed terms," said one Western diplomat.
"They had a nice, cosy, friendly state friendship that broke down (in the 1960s) and there is nothing in this that really shows that things are so different now," he said.

President Jiang Zemin of China and his Russian counterpart, Boris Yeltsin, joined forces on Wednesday in opposing the domination of one superpower in the post-Cold War world and to build a partnership after decades of mistrust.
The two leaders hugged, smiled and signed the declaration in the gilded hall of the Grand Kremlin palace.

It is the latest in a string of treaties and communiques signed by the two nations since the 1689 Treaty of Nerchinsk -- China's first agreement with a Western power and one of many that crumbled under the territorial or political ambitions of one side or the other.
Diplomats said the declaration appeared clearly intended as a message to the United States that it could not monopolise the world stage as the only superpower.

"China in particular sees the United States as a superpower in decline against the rise of several other poles of power -- China, Russia, Western Europe and maybe ASEAN (the Association of Southeast Asian Nations)," the first diplomat said.

Differing degrees of anxiety in Russia and China -- with Moscow more concerned about the expansion of NATO (the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation) and China worried about the United States -- could prevent development of a China-Russia axis, diplomats said.

Beijing and Moscow could see mutual benefits from such a declaration because both were interested in the decline of the United States as a superpower that could limit their development, another diplomat said.
"Whether their friendship lasts beyond that, we will have to see," he said.

Chinese academics praised the declaration, carried in full by the People's Daily, mouthpiece of the Communist Party, as a triumph for China and for President and party chief Jiang and as a signal of warming ties.
"There have been twists and turns in the history of Sino-Russian relations but the tendency of future ties is good," said one Russia specialist at Beijing University.

Despite the shadow of history and doubts about the long-term health of the declaration, diplomats said the fact that the two sides had been able to reach such an agreement was testament to the rapidly deepening friendship between the former bitter rivals for leadership of the socialist world.
"The Sino-Russia relationship is in very good shape, which is something pretty unusual for China," the first diplomat said. "The Chinese see in Russia a soul mate in the face of American domination."
China also sees advantages for trade, albeit limited, and has its eye on Russian technology, diplomats said.
However, years of suspicion cast their shadow and could dilute both sides' commitment to the declaration if new tensions emerge over old border disputes, they said.
"China is concerned about Russian revanchism in the Far East," the first Western diplomat said.
Chinese memories of Russian expansion that resulted in that first of many treaties in 1689 may still linger.
